newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade minister may skip WTO Singapore meet.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade minister may skip WTO Singapore meet.

text.p: Japan's aspiration to be a major player at a global trade forum in Singapore next month could be punctured if, as appears possible, its trade chief pulls out due to a domestic scandal.

A Trade Ministry spokesman said on Thursday that Trade Minister Shinji Sato would likely make at best a brief appearance at a gathering of ministers from the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Singapore on December 9-13 because of the pressures of parliamentary business.
Sato is expected to face harsh opposition questioning in parliament about a scandal linking his officials to an oil dealer arrested this month for suspected tax evasion.
"The minister's schedule has not been decided, but if he goes, it might be only briefly. And he might not be able to go at all," the Trade Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
Sato, who took the post in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's cabinet formed earlier this month, said on Tuesday he had begun a probe into possible corruption at the ministry.

The affair is the latest in a series of scandals involving bureaucrats which in the past week have toppled a deputy health minister and a provincial governor. The scandals have put a harsh spotlight on Japan's elite bureaucrats, once regarded as the architects of the nation's economic success.

Millionaire oil wholesaler Junichi Izui, arrested on charges of evading 310 million yen ($2.74 million) in taxes, has boasted of close ties to politicians and bureaucrats whom he allegedly wined and dined.

He also donated millions of yen to high-ranking politicians across the political spectrum, including key members of Hashimoto's new cabinet. The investigation of Izui is focusing on the hefty commissions he received for oil transactions involving Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Mitsui Mining Co Ltd.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda is also likely to make his WTO appearance short due to parliamentary business, although no scandal has surfaced at his ministry, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Japanese trade officials, who have been beating the multilateral trade drum for years, seemed disappointed but resigned to Tokyo's potentially low profile in Singapore.
"Of course the meeting is very important, but for politicians, parliament has to take precedence," one said.

Japan has touted the WTO as the preferred forum for settling disputes with trade partners, including the United States, instead of dealing with feuds in two-way talks, often under the threat of American sanctions.
WTO envoys in Geneva, meanwhile, have been battling to resolve strong differences over the text of a declaration to be issued by the ministers in Singapore.
Key developing countries are opposed to any discussion, especially at Singapore, of linkage between trade and investment, trade and competition, and labour standards.
The four major trading powers -- the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada -- are not agreed on which of these three issues should be on the WTO agenda.

Japan also supports a U.S.-backed plan to have free trade in the huge information technology market by the turn of the century, and would like to see progress towards China being admitted to the world trade body.
